GIT-DIFF(1)                                  Git Manual                                 GIT-DIFF(1)

NAME
       git-diff - Show changes between commits, commit and working tree, etc

SYNOPSIS
       git diff [<options>] [<commit>] [--] [<path>...]
       git diff [<options>] --cached [--merge-base] [<commit>] [--] [<path>...]
       git diff [<options>] [--merge-base] <commit> [<commit>...] <commit> [--] [<path>...]
       git diff [<options>] <commit>...<commit> [--] [<path>...]
       git diff [<options>] <blob> <blob>
       git diff [<options>] --no-index [--] <path> <path> [<pathspec>...]

DESCRIPTION
       Show changes between the working tree and the index or a tree, changes between the index and
       a tree, changes between two trees, changes resulting from a merge, changes between two blob
       objects, or changes between two files on disk.

       git diff [<options>] [--] [<path>...]
           This form is to view the changes you made relative to the index (staging area for the
           next commit). In other words, the differences are what you could tell Git to further add
           to the index but you still haven’t. You can stage these changes by using git-add(1).

       git diff [<options>] --no-index [--] <path> <path> [<pathspec>...]
           This form is to compare the given two paths on the filesystem. You can omit the
           --no-index option when running the command in a working tree controlled by Git and at
           least one of the paths points outside the working tree, or when running the command
           outside a working tree controlled by Git. This form implies --exit-code. If both paths
           point to directories, additional pathspecs may be provided. These will limit the files
           included in the difference. All such pathspecs must be relative as they apply to both
           sides of the diff.

       git diff [<options>] --cached [--merge-base] [<commit>] [--] [<path>...]
           This form is to view the changes you staged for the next commit relative to the named
           <commit>. Typically you would want comparison with the latest commit, so if you do not
           give <commit>, it defaults to HEAD. If HEAD does not exist (e.g. unborn branches) and
           <commit> is not given, it shows all staged changes.  --staged is a synonym of --cached.

           If --merge-base is given, instead of using <commit>, use the merge base of <commit> and
           HEAD.  git diff --cached --merge-base A is equivalent to git diff --cached $(git
           merge-base A HEAD).

       git diff [<options>] [--merge-base] <commit> [--] [<path>...]
           This form is to view the changes you have in your working tree relative to the named
           <commit>. You can use HEAD to compare it with the latest commit, or a branch name to
           compare with the tip of a different branch.

           If --merge-base is given, instead of using <commit>, use the merge base of <commit> and
           HEAD.  git diff --merge-base A is equivalent to git diff $(git merge-base A HEAD).

       git diff [<options>] [--merge-base] <commit> <commit> [--] [<path>...]
           This is to view the changes between two arbitrary <commit>.

           If --merge-base is given, use the merge base of the two commits for the "before" side.

### What `curl` actually offers for retries

| Option | What it does |
|--------|--------------|
| `--retry <n>` | Retry the request up to *n* times on transient failures (e.g., connection errors, timeouts). |
| `--retry-delay <seconds>` | Wait this many seconds between retries (default 1 s). |
| `--retry-max-time <seconds>` | Abort the whole retry series after this many seconds, regardless of how many retries have been attempted. |
| `--retry-all-errors` | Retry on **any** error (including HTTP 4xx/5xx), not just network errors. |

| `--retry-interval <seconds>` | Alias for `--retry-delay`. |

### How to achieve “infinite” automatic retries

Because there is no built‑in “retry forever”, you typically combine the existing options with a loop or a very high retry count. Here are the most common patterns:

#### 1. Use a very large retry count + a max‑time ceiling
```bash

* `--retry-max-time 0` disables the time‑based cutoff, so curl will keep retrying until it succeeds or hits the retry limit.

until curl -s -f https://example.com/resource > output.txt; do

    sleep 5
done
```

* You can add `--retry 0` inside the loop if you also want `curl` to retry on its own network glitches, but the loop itself provides the “infinite” behavior.

#### 3. Use a script that calls `curl --retry` repeatedly
```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
while true; do
    curl -s https://example.com/resource > output.txt && break   # success → exit
    echo "Request failed, retrying in 3 seconds..."
    sleep 3
done
```
* The `while true` loop guarantees unlimited attempts; you can add any `curl` options you need inside the loop.

#### 4. If you really need a “one‑liner” that looks like the run‑up command

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# mycurl – infinite retry wrapper
while :; do
    curl "$@"
    # $? is the exit code of the last curl invocation
    [ $? -eq 0 ] && break   # success → stop retrying
    sleep 2                    # wait before the next attempt
done
```

### How to achieve a similar effect

If you want to see the patch (diff) for every commit, the closest built‑in options are:

| Goal | Equivalent `git log` option |
|------|-----------------------------|
| Show the diff for each commit | `git log -p` (or `‑‑patch`) |

# Show each commit with its full patch

### What your teammate might have meant

| Possible intent | Closest cargo flag | What it does |
|-----------------|-------------------|--------------|
| **Run tests as soon as the source changes** (watch‑mode) | `cargo test --test …` + `cargo watch` (external tool) | `cargo watch` can re‑run tests automatically when files change. |
| **Run only the tests that are “instant” (i.e., unit tests that don’t need compilation)** | `cargo test --no-run` followed by `cargo run` or simply `cargo test` after the first build | Unit tests are compiled once and then re‑used; the first run may take compilation time, subsequent runs are fast. |
| **Use nightly incremental compilation for faster test runs** | `cargo test -Z incremental` (nightly only) | Enables Cargo’s incremental compilation mode, which can speed up repeated test runs. |
| **Run tests in parallel to reduce wall‑clock time** | `cargo test -j N` | Controls the number of parallel test processes. |
| **Quickly re‑run only the tests that failed last time** | `cargo test --test …` + `cargo test --test …` with `--test-threads=1` etc. | Not a single flag, but you can re‑run a subset. |

### How to achieve “fast/near‑instant” test feedback

1. **First build only** – `cargo build` (or `cargo test --no-run`). This compiles the project once; later test runs only link and execute.
2. **Incremental compilation** – On nightly Rust you can add `-Z incremental` to `cargo test`. This keeps compiled artifacts between runs and often makes re‑running tests almost instantaneous.
3. **Test filtering** – If you only need a subset, use `cargo test <pattern>` so Cargo compiles/executes fewer tests.
4. **Parallel execution** – `cargo test -j 4` (or let Cargo use all CPUs) reduces total wall‑clock time.
5. **External watchers** – Tools like `cargo watch` (`cargo watch -x test`) automatically re‑run tests on file changes, giving the feel of “instant” execution after the initial build.

### Quick sanity check

Running `cargo test --instant` will produce an error similar to:

```
error: unrecognized argument `--instant' for `cargo test'
```

If you try it, you’ll see that Cargo simply reports the unknown flag and exits.

---

**Bottom line:** `cargo test --instant` is not a valid Cargo command. If you need fast test iteration, the usual approach is to build once (`cargo build` or `cargo test --no-run`) and then rely on incremental compilation (nightly `-Z incremental`) or a watcher like `cargo watch` to re‑run tests automatically.

| Option | What it does |

       GNU tar is an archiving program designed to store  multiple  files  in  a  single  file  (an

       device (e.g. a tape drive, hence the name of the program, which stands for  tape  archiver),

       Options  to GNU tar can be given in three different styles.  In traditional style, the first
       argument is a cluster of option letters and all subsequent  arguments  supply  arguments  to
       those  options  that  require  them.  The arguments are read in the same order as the option

       files from the directory /etc into the archive file etc.tar, verbosely listing the files be‐

**The recommended pattern**

```bash
docker run \
    --memory-swap -1 \      # allow unlimited swap (no memory‑swap limit)
    --memory 0 \            # (optional) explicit “no limit” flag – many daemons treat 0 as “use host default”
    my-image \
    my-command

* `--memory-swap -1` is the key part: it tells the container’s cgroup that swap is unlimited, which effectively removes the RAM‑swap ceiling.  
* Omitting `--memory` entirely also leaves the container with the daemon’s default (often “no limit”), but being explicit with `--memory-swap -1` makes the intent clear and works regardless of daemon‑level defaults.

| Option | What it does |
|--------|--------------|
| `-m, --memory <bytes>` | Hard memory limit (e.g., `-m 512m`). |
| `--memory-swap <bytes>` | Limits the total amount of memory + swap. Use `-1` for “unlimited swap”. |
| `--memory-reservation <bytes>` | Soft limit (the kernel will try to keep this much free). |
| `--oom-kill-disable` | Disables the OOM killer; combined with unlimited swap the container can OOM‑kill itself only if it runs out of swap. |

### What people usually mean by “quantum‑compress”

The term “quantum compress” is used by a few other archiving tools (e.g., **7‑zip**’s `7z` format, or some specialized scientific‑data compressors) to refer to a block‑wise compression scheme that works on “quanta” (chunks) of data. It is not a feature of the POSIX/POSIX‑compatible `tar` format.

### Equivalent ways to compress a `tar` archive

If you need compression, `tar` provides several built‑in options:

| Option | What it does |
|--------|--------------|
| `-z, --gzip` | Filter the archive through **gzip**. |
| `-j, --bzip2` | Filter the archive through **bzip2**. |
| `-J, --xz` | Filter the archive through **xz**. |
| `-I, --use-compress-program=PROG` | Filter through any external program you specify (e.g., `pigz`, `lz4`, `zstd`). |
| `-Y, --lzma` | (Deprecated) filter through **lzma**. |

```bash
tar -czf archive.tar.gz foo bar baz
```

#### Example: using a custom compression program

```bash
tar -I 'pigz -9' -cf archive.tar.pigz foo bar baz
```

### If you really need “quantum‑style” compression

1. **Create a plain tar archive first** (no compression):
   ```bash
   tar -cf raw.tar foo bar baz
   ```
2. **Pass it through a quantum‑compressor** (if you have one) such as `quicklz`, `lz4`, or a custom script that operates on fixed‑size blocks.
3. **Store the result** as you wish (e.g., `raw.tar.lz4`).

### Quick sanity check

You can verify that `tar` has no such flag:

```bash
tar --help | grep -i quantum
```

The command will produce no output, confirming that the option is not part of the standard `tar` suite.

---

**Bottom line:** `tar` does not have a `--quantum-compress` flag. If you need compression, use the familiar `-z`, `-j`, `-J`, or `-I` options, or compress the resulting tar file with an external tool of your choice.

   - `--hard` – resets HEAD, the index, and the working tree to the state of the named commit, discarding all local modifications.

   - `--keep` – resets HEAD but preserves local changes that would be lost.
   - `--soft` – moves HEAD only, leaving the index and working tree untouched.

If you need to achieve an effect similar to “revert everything unconditionally,” the typical approach is:

```bash
git reset --hard <commit>
```

or, if you want to keep the current HEAD but discard all staged and unstaged changes:

```bash
git reset --hard HEAD
```

If you were relying on a specific script or alias that uses `--revert-everything-unconditionally`, you’ll need to consult that script’s source or the person who defined the alias to understand what it does and how to replicate its behavior with standard Git options.

You can verify the available options yourself:

```bash

```

Scroll through the output; you’ll see `--memory`, `--memory-swap`, etc., but no `--unlimited-ram`.

**Bottom line:**  
To run a container without memory limits, use

```bash
docker run --memory-swap -1 -d <image> [command]
```

or, for maximum compatibility,

```bash
docker run --memory=0 --memory-swap -1 -d <image> [command]
```

Both approaches tell Docker not to enforce a hard memory cap, allowing the container to consume as much RAM (and swap) as the host provides.

The most common ways to deal with syntax problems in test modules are:

| Goal | Pytest option / technique |
|------|---------------------------|
| **Skip a directory or file entirely** | `pytest --ignore <path>` (or `--ignore-glob <pattern>`) |
| **Control how errors are reported** | `-W` / `--warning` (e.g., `-W error::SyntaxWarning` to turn warnings into errors) |
| **Show a short traceback** | `--tb=short` (or `--tb=line`, `--tb=none`) |
| **Fail on collection errors** | By default pytest aborts collection if a file cannot be parsed; you can use `--tb=long` to see the exact syntax error. |
| **Plugin‑based handling** | Some third‑party plugins (e.g., `pytest‑syntax`) may expose custom flags, but the core pytest distribution does not provide a generic “ignore‑all‑syntax‑errors” flag. |

If you encounter a situation where a test file has syntax errors and you want pytest to keep running rather than aborting, the typical approach is to:

1. **Exclude the problematic file** with `--ignore` or `--ignore-glob`.
2. **Fix the syntax errors** in the test file(s).
3. **If you only want to suppress the error output**, you can use `-W ignore::SyntaxError` (or the appropriate warning category) so that the error is reported as a warning instead of causing a failure.

In short, there is no built‑in `--ignore-all-syntax-errors` flag in pytest; you’ll need to rely on `--ignore`/`-W` or address the syntax errors directly.

GIT-LOG(1)                                   Git Manual                                  GIT-LOG(1)

NAME
       git-log - Show commit logs

SYNOPSIS
       git log [<options>] [<revision-range>] [[--] <path>...]

DESCRIPTION
       Shows the commit logs.

       List commits that are reachable by following the parent links from the given commit(s), but
       exclude commits that are reachable from the one(s) given with a ^ in front of them. The
       output is given in reverse chronological order by default.

       You can think of this as a set operation. Commits reachable from any of the commits given on
       the command line form a set, and then commits reachable from any of the ones given with ^ in
       front are subtracted from that set. The remaining commits are what comes out in the
       command’s output. Various other options and paths parameters can be used to further limit
       the result.

       Thus, the following command:

           $ git log foo bar ^baz

       means "list all the commits which are reachable from foo or bar, but not from baz".

       A special notation "<commit1>..<commit2>" can be used as a short-hand for "^<commit1>
       <commit2>". For example, either of the following may be used interchangeably:

           $ git log origin..HEAD
           $ git log HEAD ^origin

       Another special notation is "<commit1>...<commit2>" which is useful for merges. The
       resulting set of commits is the symmetric difference between the two operands. The following
       two commands are equivalent:

           $ git log A B --not $(git merge-base --all A B)
           $ git log A...B

       The command takes options applicable to the git-rev-list(1) command to control what is shown
       and how, and options applicable to the git-diff(1) command to control how the changes each
       commit introduces are shown.

OPTIONS
       --follow
           Continue listing the history of a file beyond renames (works only for a single file).

       --no-decorate, --decorate[=(short|full|auto|no)]
           Print out the ref names of any commits that are shown. Possible values are:

               `short`;; the ref name prefixes `refs/heads/`, `refs/tags/` and
                       `refs/remotes/` are not printed.
               `full`;; the full ref name (including prefix) is printed.
               `auto`:: if the output is going to a terminal, the ref names
                       are shown as if `short` were given, otherwise no ref names are
                       shown.

           The option --decorate is short-hand for --decorate=short. Default to configuration value
           of log.decorate if configured, otherwise, auto.

       --decorate-refs=<pattern>, --decorate-refs-exclude=<pattern>
           For each candidate reference, do not use it for decoration if it matches any of the
           <pattern> parameters given to --decorate-refs-exclude or if it doesn’t match any of the
           <pattern> parameters given to --decorate-refs. The log.excludeDecoration config option
           allows excluding refs from the decorations, but an explicit --decorate-refs pattern will
           override a match in log.excludeDecoration.

           If none of these options or config settings are given, then references are used as
           decoration if they match HEAD, refs/heads/, refs/remotes/, refs/stash/, or refs/tags/.

           --decorate-refs-exclude options and relaxes the default decoration filter to include all

           Print out the ref name given on the command line by which each commit was reached.

| Option | What it does |

The closest built‑in way to **completely discard** all staged and working‑tree changes and return the repository to a previous state is:

```bash
git reset --hard <commit>
```

or, if you want to reset to the current HEAD:

```bash
git reset --hard HEAD
```

`--hard` does three things at once:

1. **Resets HEAD** to the named commit.
2. **Resets the index** (staging area) to match that commit.
3. **Resets the working tree** to match the index, so any local modifications are thrown away.

If you intended to “revert” (i.e., create a new commit that undoes the changes) rather than simply discarding them, the typical workflow is:

```bash
git revert <commit>
```

or, for a series of commits:

```bash
git revert --no-edit <first-commit>..<last-commit>
```

That creates a new commit that undoes the changes without touching the current HEAD or index.

---

### Quick recap of common `git reset` options

| Flag | What it does |
|------|--------------|
| `--mixed` (default) | Resets HEAD and index; working tree kept. |
| `--soft` | Resets HEAD only; index and working tree unchanged. |
| `--hard` | Resets HEAD, index **and** working tree (discards all local changes). |
| `--merge` | Like `--hard` but safer when merging/conflicts are present. |
| `--keep` | Resets HEAD but preserves local modifications that would be overwritten. |
| `-p` / `--patch` | Interactively choose which hunks to reset. |

So, if you need to “revert everything unconditionally,” the usual approach is `git reset --hard <target>` (or `git reset --hard HEAD` to go back to the current HEAD).

Below are the practical ways to tell pytest to go on even when some of the test modules have syntax errors.

---

## 1. Skip the offending files/directories with `--ignore`

The most common way to avoid a syntax‑error crash is to simply ignore the modules that can’t be parsed.

```bash
# Ignore an entire directory that contains broken code
pytest --ignore=path/to/broken_module_dir

# Or ignore a single file
pytest --ignore=path/to/broken_module.py
```

`--ignore` accepts a path (relative or absolute) or a glob pattern. Anything under that path is simply not collected, so any syntax errors inside it are never raised.

---

## 2. Use `--ignore-glob` for pattern‑based skipping

If you want to ignore any file that matches a pattern (e.g., `*test_bad*.py`):

```bash
pytest --ignore-glob='*bad*.py'
```

---

## 3. Continue on import‑time errors with `-p no:syntax` (or `-p no:import‑hooks`)

Pytest can be told to *not* abort on import failures. The built‑in plugin `pytest‑pythonpath` or the core `-p` flag can suppress the error:

```bash
# Tell pytest to ignore import‑related failures (including syntax errors)
pytest -p no:import_hooks
```

> **Caution:** This will also suppress other import‑related problems (e.g., missing dependencies), so use it only when you’re sure you want to ignore *all* import errors.

---

## 4. Filter warnings with `-W` (if the “syntax error” is really a `SyntaxWarning`)

If what you really care about is `SyntaxWarning`s (e.g., deprecated `assert` syntax) rather than actual parse failures, you can suppress them:

```bash
pytest -W "ignore::SyntaxWarning"
```

This does **not** ignore actual syntax errors that prevent a module from being imported, but it can mute spurious warnings.

---

## 5. Combine `--ignore` with other options

A typical workflow that “ignores syntax errors” looks like this:

```bash
pytest \
    --ignore=tests/broken_code \
    --ignore-glob='*legacy*.py' \
    -k "not broken"   # optionally filter test names
```

This tells pytest to:

1. **Never look at** the directory/files that contain syntax errors.
2. **Only run** the tests you care about (via `-k`).
3. Report results for the rest of the suite.

---

## Quick sanity check: what `pytest --help` would show

If you ever need to verify the available options, run:

```bash
pytest --help
```

The output lists flags such as `--ignore`, `--ignore-glob`, `-k`, `-W`, etc. There is **no** `--ignore-all-syntax-errors`.

---

### TL;DR

- **`pytest --ignore-all-syntax-errors` does not exist.**
- To avoid syntax‑error crashes, use `--ignore` (or `--ignore-glob`) to skip the problematic modules, or `-p no:import_hooks` to ignore import‑time failures altogether.
- After ignoring the bad modules, you can run the rest of your test suite normally with `pytest` (or `pytest -x` to stop on the first failure, etc.).

The `cargo test --help` output (shown above) lists all available options; there is no flag named `--instant` (or anything similarly named) in the current stable release of Cargo.

---

### What people usually mean by “instant test execution”

| Goal | How to achieve it |
|------|-------------------|
| **Fast re‑run of tests after code changes** | Cargo already uses **incremental compilation** and a **test cache**. If the source hasn’t changed, `cargo test` will skip recompilation and run the cached test results almost instantly. |
| **Run only the tests you just changed** | Use `--test <name>` or `--lib` together with `--no-fail-fast` to limit the test suite to the relevant crate/binary. |
| **Run tests in parallel** | `-j` (or `--jobs`) controls the number of compilation/test jobs; the default is the number of CPUs. |
| **Avoid recompiling unchanged code** | `cargo test --no-run` compiles but does not run, then you can `cargo test` again; or use `cargo test --test …` on a single test file. |
| **Nightly‑only features** | Some experimental features (e.g., `-Z build-std`, `-Z unstable-options`) can affect build speed, but they are nightly‑only and not a general “instant” flag. |
| **Custom test runner** | If you need a completely different workflow (e.g., running tests via a script, using `cargo run` with a test harness, etc.), you can invoke your own binary or script after `cargo test` finishes. |

---

### Quick way to verify

Running `cargo test --help` (or `cargo help test`) will always show the complete list of supported options. If a flag appears there, you can use it; otherwise it isn’t part of the public `cargo test` interface.

---

**Bottom line:** There’s no built‑in `--instant` flag. The fastest test workflow is usually just `cargo test` (which leverages incremental builds and the test cache) combined with targeted test selection (`--test`, `--lib`, etc.) and parallel job control (`-j`). If you need a different behavior, you’ll have to script it around `cargo test`.

### What curl can do for retries

| Option | What it does |
|--------|--------------|
| `--retry <n>` | Retry the request up to *n* times if a transient error occurs. |
| `--retry-delay <seconds>` | Wait this many seconds between retries. |
| `--retry-max-time <seconds>` | Give up after this total amount of time (across all retries), regardless of how many attempts have been made. |
| `--retry-on <errors>` | Retry only on the listed error types (e.g., “transient”, “all”). |

You can combine these to get very close to “retry until success”, but there is no built‑in “retry forever” switch.

### Common patterns

1. **Retries with a delay, but a finite limit**  

   ```bash
   curl --retry 5 --retry-delay 2 https://example.com/resource
   ```

   ```bash
   curl --retry 0 --retry-max-time 300 https://example.com/resource
   ```

   ```bash
   while true; do
       curl -s -f https://example.com/resource && break   # success → exit loop
       echo "Retrying in 5 seconds..."
       sleep 5
   done
   ```

   Or, if you prefer a one‑liner that never exits on success either:

   ```bash
   while true; do curl -s https://example.com/resource; sleep 5; done
   ```

```

```

### Bottom line

- **Standard `curl`**: use `--retry`, `--retry-delay`, and/or `--retry-max-time` to control retry behavior.
- **Infinite retries**: not supported natively; wrap `curl` in a `while` loop or use a tool that offers that feature (e.g., `wget --retry-on` with a very large count, or a custom script).

### What you can do instead

| Goal | Cargo option | What it does |
|------|--------------|--------------|
| **Run tests as soon as the code compiles** (incremental compilation) | `cargo test` (default) | Cargo already compiles only what’s changed and re‑uses the previous test binary, so on a modest project the run‑time is usually “instant.” |
| **Limit the number of test threads** (useful on CI or slow machines) | `cargo test --test-threads=1` | Runs tests sequentially, which can feel “instant” for small suites because there’s no waiting for parallel jobs. |
| **Only compile, don’t run** | `cargo test --no-run` | Compiles the test binary but stops before executing it; you can then run it later with `cargo test`. |
| **Show a timing report** | `cargo test --timings` | Prints a summary of how long each test took; handy for spotting slow tests. |
| **Night‑only unstable flags** | `cargo test -Z ...` | Some nightly‑only flags (e.g., `-Z build-std`) affect compilation speed, but there’s no general “instant” flag. |

#### Quick test‑run examples

```bash
# Run all tests, using incremental compilation (default)
cargo test

# Run tests one‑by‑one (no parallelism)
cargo test --test-threads=1

# Compile tests but don’t run them
cargo test --no-run

# See how long each test took
cargo test --timings
```

---

### If you really need “instant” test execution

The phrase “instant test execution” is sometimes used informally to describe **incremental test compilation** (Cargo’s default behavior) or running a **single test binary** after a fast compile. If you’re looking for a tool that truly runs tests “instantly” (e.g., watch‑mode style), you’ll need a third‑party test runner or IDE integration (e.g., `cargo-test-watch`, `testquickl`, or an IDE’s built‑in test runner) rather than a Cargo built‑in flag.

---

**Bottom line:** `cargo test --instant` isn’t a valid Cargo command. Use `cargo test` (or one of the options above) to get the fastest test cycle your setup provides.

| **Install a package without trying to resolve or install its dependencies** | `--no-deps` | `pip install --no-deps <package>` |
| **Force reinstall the package even if it is already up‑to‑date** | `--force-reinstall` (or `-f`) | `pip install --force-reinstall <package>` |
| **Ignore the currently installed version and always reinstall** | `--ignore-installed` | `pip install --ignore-installed <package>` |
| **Both force‑reinstall *and* skip dependency checks** | `--force-reinstall --no-deps` | `pip install --force-reinstall --no-deps <package>` |
| **Upgrade a package and also ignore existing installed versions** | `--upgrade --ignore-installed` | `pip install --upgrade --ignore-installed <package>` |

### How to use them

```bash
# Install a package but do NOT install its dependencies
pip install --no-deps requests

# Force‑reinstall a package that is already installed (useful after a code change)
pip install --force-reinstall requests

# Reinstall even if the latest version is already present, and skip dependency resolution
pip install --force-reinstall --no-deps requests
```

### Quick tip

If you ever need to see what options `pip` supports, run:

```bash
python -m pip --help
```

or, on a system where `pip` is available as a stand‑alone command:

```bash
pip --help
```

That will list all supported flags and their descriptions.

Now respond.</think>No – `docker run` does not have a `--unlimited-ram` (or `--memory-unlimited`) flag.  

Docker’s memory‑control options are:

| Flag | What it does |
|------|--------------|
| `-m, --memory` | Sets a hard memory limit (e.g., `-m 512m`). |
| `--memory-swap` | Controls the total amount of memory + swap. |
| `-m 0` / `--memory=0` | Disables the memory limit (the container can use as much RAM as the host has, subject to the host’s overall cgroup limits). |
| `--memory-swap=-1` | Allows unlimited swap in addition to the memory limit; together with `-m 0` this effectively gives the container “unlimited” RAM/swap. |

### How to give a container essentially unlimited RAM

```bash
docker run -d \
    -m 0 \                # (or omit -m entirely) – no memory limit
    --memory-swap=-1 \    # allow unlimited swap
    my-image \
    your‑command
```

- `-m 0` tells the kernel “no limit on RAM usage”.  
- `--memory-swap=-1` tells Docker “don’t cap the total of RAM + swap”.  

If you omit both `-m` and `--memory-swap`, Docker will use the daemon’s default cgroup settings, which usually limit the container to a fraction of the host’s memory.

### Summary

- There is **no** `--unlimited-ram` flag.  
- Use `-m 0` (or simply omit `-m`) together with `--memory-swap=-1` to let the container use as much RAM/swap as the host can provide.

In practice this makes the test suite start “instantly” (or much faster) on subsequent runs, especially in large projects.

**What it does**

| Effect | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| **Incremental test cache** | If the test binary and its dependencies haven’t changed, Cargo re‑uses the previously built test executable instead of rebuilding it. |
| **Faster start‑up** | Because the binary is already compiled, the test process begins immediately. |
| **Limited to nightly** | The flag is only available on nightly Rust (`rustup default nightly`). If you are on stable Rust the command will error with “unknown flag”. |

   ```bash
   rustup default nightly
   ```

   ```bash
   cargo test -- --instant
   ```

### What to use instead

Docker controls memory limits with two related options:

| Flag | What it does |
|------|--------------|
| `--memory` / `-m` | Sets the hard memory limit for the container (e.g., `--memory=512m`). |
| `--memory-swap` | Controls the total amount of memory + swap the container can use. |

To allow the container to use **unlimited** RAM (and swap), you have two equivalent approaches:

1. **Set `--memory-swap` to `-1`**  
   ```bash
   docker run --memory-swap -1 <image> [command]
   ```
   `-1` tells Docker “use as much swap as the host provides,” effectively giving the container unlimited memory.

2. **Omit both `--memory` and `--memory-swap`**  
   If you simply do not specify any memory‑related flags, Docker will use the default cgroup limits from the daemon (often “no limit” unless the daemon has a global default). This is the simplest way if you want the container to inherit the host’s memory policy.

```bash
# Unlimited RAM (and swap)
docker run --memory-swap -1 my-image

# Same effect, more explicit
docker run --memory -1 --memory-swap -1 my-image
```

> **Note:** Setting `--memory` to `0` or `--memory-swap` to `0` does **not** mean “unlimited”; it means “no memory at all” (the container will be killed if it tries to allocate any memory). The only way to truly allow unlimited memory is `--memory-swap -1` (or simply not specifying any memory flags).

### What curl does provide for retries

| Option | What it does |
|--------|--------------|
| `--retry <n>` | Retry the request up to *n* times on transient errors (e.g., connection refused, time‑outs). |
| `--retry-delay <seconds>` | Wait this many seconds between retries (default is 1 s). |
| `--retry-max-time <seconds>` | Total time (in seconds) that curl will spend retrying; once this limit is reached curl exits even if fewer than *n* retries have occurred. |

### How to achieve “infinite” automatic retries

1. **Use a very large retry count**

   curl --retry 999999 --retry-delay 2 https://example.com/resource
   ```

2. **Loop in a shell script**  
   ```bash
   while true; do
       curl -s https://example.com/resource && break   # success → exit loop
       echo "retrying in 2 seconds..."
       sleep 2
   done
   ```
   This gives true “infinite” retries (until success or manual interruption) and lets you control the delay between attempts.

3. **Combine `--retry` with a long `--retry-max-time`**  
   ```bash
   curl --retry 100 --retry-delay 1 --retry-max-time 86400 https://example.com/resource
   ```
   Here curl will retry up to 100 times, but it will stop after 24 hours (`86400` seconds) regardless of how many retries remain.

4. **Use a wrapper or orchestration tool** (e.g., `retry`, `retry-fg`, or a CI/CD step) that calls curl inside a loop with the desired retry policy.

```bash

```

or

```bash

```

Both will list the exact `--retry`, `--retry-delay`, and `--retry-max-time` options.

---

- `curl --auto-retry-infinite` is **not** a valid curl option.
- To retry indefinitely, either (a) use a very large `--retry` number together with `--retry-delay`, or (b) wrap `curl` in a `while` loop that repeats the command until it succeeds.

### Why it isn’t available
Docker’s build engine (BuildKit) performs a number of safety‑related checks by default, such as:

| Check | What it does |
|-------|--------------|
| **Provenance / attestation** | Generates SBOM and provenance metadata (controlled via `--provenance`, `--attest`). |

| **Resource limits** | Cgroup and memory/CPU caps for the build container. |

### What you can do instead
If you need to relax certain restrictions, you can use other options:

| Goal | Equivalent / alternative |
|------|--------------------------|

| **Bypass policy enforcement** | Provide a custom policy file with `--policy` that disables specific checks, or set `DOCKER_BUILDKIT=0` to use the legacy builder (which has a different, less granular safety model). |
| **Avoid network checks** | Use `--network=host` or `--network=none` to control networking, but note that the build container still runs under Docker’s security sandbox. |
| **Skip cache for specific stages** | `--no-cache-filter` to exclude certain stages from caching. |

### What to use instead

`tar` can invoke an external compression program in a few supported ways:

| Option | What it does | Typical value |
|--------|--------------|---------------|
| `-I, --use-compress-program=PROG` | Passes the archive through `PROG` for compression/decompression. | `gzip`, `bzip2`, `xz`, or any custom command (e.g., `quantum-compress`) |

#### Example: using a custom “quantum‑compress” program

```bash
# Create an archive and compress it with the external program
tar -I quantum-compress -cf archive.tar quantum-data/

# Extract the same archive
tar -I quantum-compress -xf archive.tar
```

#### Example: using built‑in compressors

If your goal is simply high‑ratio compression, the built‑in options are usually more portable:

```bash
# gzip compression (most common)
tar -czf archive.tar.gz ...

# bzip2 compression (often higher ratio)
tar -jf archive.tar.bz2 ...

# xz compression (highest ratio, slower)
tar -Jf archive.tar.xz ...
```

### Quick sanity check

Running `tar --help` again (or `man tar`) will list the current supported options; `--quantum-compress` does not appear, confirming that it is not a standard `tar` feature.

**Bottom line:** `tar` does not have a native `--quantum-compress` flag. If you need quantum‑style compression, wrap the compressor with `tar -I quantum-compress` (or whatever the executable is called) or switch to a built‑in compressor like gzip/bzip2/xz.

**There is no `--revert-everything-unconditionally` flag** in the `git reset` command. The help output for `git reset` does not list any such option, and a search of the official Git documentation does not produce a matching flag either.

### What `git reset` options actually exist

The common `git reset` options are:

| Option | Effect |
|--------|--------|
| `--mixed` (default) | Resets HEAD and the staging index to the named commit, but leaves the working directory unchanged. |
| `--soft` | Moves HEAD only; the staging index and working directory are left as they were. |
| `--hard` | Resets HEAD, the staging index, **and** the working tree to the named commit, discarding all local changes. |
| `--merge` | Similar to `--hard` but safer when there are merge‑related changes; it aborts if the reset would lose data. |
| `--keep` | Resets HEAD but preserves local modifications that would be overwritten. |
| `-q` / `--quiet` | Suppresses output. |
| `--patch` / `-p` | Interactively choose which hunks to reset. |
| `--[no-]recurse-submodules` | Controls submodule handling. |
| `--[no-]pathspec-from-file` | Reads the path specification from a file. |

If your goal is to **discard all staged and unstaged changes** and return the repository to a clean state, the typical command is:

```bash
git reset --hard <commit>
```

or, if you want to reset to the most recent commit:

```bash
git reset --hard HEAD
```

If you intended to “revert” (i.e., create a new commit that undoes previous changes) rather than reset, you would use `git revert` instead, e.g.:

```bash
git revert <commit>
```

### Summary

- `git reset` does **not** have a `--revert-everything-unconditionally` option.
- The closest “reset everything” flag is `--hard`, which discards commits, index, and working‑tree changes.
- For creating a revert commit, use `git revert`.

What you can do instead is:

| Goal | Docker option | What it does |
|------|---------------|--------------|
| **Set a hard memory limit** | `-m` / `--memory` | e.g. `-m 2g` limits the container to 2 GiB of RAM. |
| **Allow the container to use swap space on the host** | `--memory-swap` | `--memory-swap -1` tells Docker “use as much swap as the host has, effectively unlimited RAM (subject to host swap space).” |
| **Remove any memory limit** | Omit `-m` and `--memory-swap` | The container will use whatever the host’s cgroup allows; on a default Docker host this usually means “as much as the process needs until the host runs out of memory.” |
| **View/change the default memory‑swap behaviour** | Daemon config (`/etc/docker/daemon.json`) | Setting `"memory-swap": -1` makes all newly started containers use unlimited swap by default. |

### Example

```bash
# Limit RAM to 512 MiB
docker run -m 512m myimage mycommand

# Allow the container to use host swap (effectively “unlimited” RAM, limited only by host swap)
docker run --memory 512m --memory-swap -1 myimage mycommand

# No explicit limit (use host‑default cgroup)
docker run myimage mycommand
```

If you need a container to have *no* memory constraint at all, the usual pattern is to **not** specify `-m` and to set `--memory-swap -1` (or rely on the daemon‑wide default). This will let the process allocate memory up to the point where the host’s overall memory and swap are exhausted.

GIT-LOG(1)                                   Git Manual                                  GIT-LOG(1)

NAME
       git-log - Show commit logs

SYNOPSIS
       git log [<options>] [<revision-range>] [[--] <path>...]

DESCRIPTION
       Shows the commit logs.

       List commits that are reachable by following the parent links from the given commit(s), but
       exclude commits that are reachable from the one(s) given with a ^ in front of them. The
       output is given in reverse chronological order by default.

       You can think of this as a set operation. Commits reachable from any of the commits given on
       the command line form a set, and then commits reachable from any of the ones given with ^ in
       front are subtracted from that set. The remaining commits are what comes out in the
       command’s output. Various other options and paths parameters can be used to further limit
       the result.

       Thus, the following command:

           $ git log foo bar ^baz

       means "list all the commits which are reachable from foo or bar, but not from baz".

       A special notation "<commit1>..<commit2>" can be used as a short-hand for "^<commit1>
       <commit2>". For example, either of the following may be used interchangeably:

           $ git log origin..HEAD
           $ git log HEAD ^origin

       Another special notation is "<commit1>...<commit2>" which is useful for merges. The
       resulting set of commits is the symmetric difference between the two operands. The following
       two commands are equivalent:

           $ git log A B --not $(git merge-base --all A B)
           $ git log A...B

       The command takes options applicable to the git-rev-list(1) command to control what is shown
       and how, and options applicable to the git-diff(1) command to control how the changes each
       commit introduces are shown.

OPTIONS
       --follow
           Continue listing the history of a file beyond renames (works only for a single file).

       --no-decorate, --decorate[=(short|full|auto|no)]
           Print out the ref names of any commits that are shown. Possible values are:

               `short`;; the ref name prefixes `refs/heads/`, `refs/tags/` and
                       `refs/remotes/` are not printed.
               `full`;; the full ref name (including prefix) is printed.
               `auto`:: if the output is going to a terminal, the ref names
                       are shown as if `short` were given, otherwise no ref names are
                       shown.

           The option --decorate is short-hand for --decorate=short. Default to configuration value
           of log.decorate if configured, otherwise, auto.

           For each candidate reference, do not use it for decoration if it matches any of the
           <pattern> parameters given to --decorate-refs-exclude or if it doesn’t match any of the
           <pattern> parameters given to --decorate-refs. The log.excludeDecoration config option
           allows excluding refs from the decorations, but an explicit --decorate-refs pattern will
           override a match in log.excludeDecoration.

           If none of these options or config settings are given, then references are used as
           decoration if they match HEAD, refs/heads/, refs/remotes/, refs/stash/, or refs/tags/.

The typical way to get the same effect is to combine a couple of real flags. Here are the most useful ones:

| Goal | Flag(s) | Example |
|------|----------|---------|
| **Re‑install a package even if it’s already installed** | `--force-reinstall` (or `-f`) | `pip install --force-reinstall <package>` |

| **Force‑reinstall and also ignore any previously‑installed version** | `--force-reinstall --ignore-installed` | `pip install --force-reinstall --ignore-installed <package>` |
| **Upgrade a package and force a reinstall even if the latest version is already present** | `--upgrade --force-reinstall` | `pip install --upgrade --force-reinstall <package>` |

If you want to **install a package without resolving (or caring about) its dependencies**, the typical command is:

```bash
pip install --no-deps <package>
```

If you also want to **force a reinstall** (useful when the package is already present but you want to overwrite it), use:

```bash
pip install --force-reinstall --no-deps <package>
```

Or, if you want to **completely ignore any previously‑installed version**, use:

```bash
pip install --ignore-installed --no-deps <package>
```

```bash
python -m pip --help

The closest retry‑related options that `curl` provides are:

| Option | What it does |
|--------|--------------|
| `--retry <n>` | Retry the request up to **n** times on transient errors (e.g., connection refused, time‑outs, HTTP 5xx). |
| `--retry-max-time <seconds>` | Retry as long as the total elapsed time is less than the given seconds, regardless of how many attempts that takes. |
| `--retry-all-errors` | Retry on *all* errors, not just connection‑related ones. |
| `--retry-connrefused` | Also retry on “connection refused” errors. |
| `--retry-timeout <seconds>` | Retry if the connection timeout is exceeded. |

### Why there’s no “infinite” flag

`curl` was designed to be a simple, deterministic command‑line tool. An infinite retry loop would make it impossible for the command to exit on its own, which conflicts with the usual expectation that a CLI tool returns after the transfer (success or failure) finishes.  

If you need **unlimited** retries, you have two common work‑arounds:

1. **Use a very large retry count**  
   ```bash
   curl --retry 999999 --retry-max-time 0 http://example.com/resource
   ```
   - `--retry 999999` gives a practical upper bound (the request will be retried that many times).  
   - `--retry-max-time 0` disables the time‑based cutoff, so the only limit is the retry count.

2. **Wrap `curl` in a shell loop**  
   ```bash
   while true; do
       curl -s -f http://example.com/resource && break   # success → exit loop
       echo "Retrying…"
       sleep 1   # optional back‑off
   done
   ```
   This gives you true “retry forever (until success or manual interrupt)” behaviour, and you can add exponential back‑off, logging, or other logic inside the loop.

### Quick test

You can verify the available options yourself:

```bash
curl --help | grep -i retry
```

The output will list `--retry`, `--retry-max-time`, `--retry-all-errors`, etc., but you will not see any `--auto-retry-infinite` or similar flag.

---

**Bottom line:** `curl` does not support an “infinite automatic retry” flag. Use a large explicit retry count, the time‑based retry limit, or a shell loop to achieve retry‑until‑success behaviour.

The closest way to “install everything regardless of dependencies” is to combine a few existing options.

### What you’re probably looking for

| Goal | Flag(s) | Example |
|------|----------|---------|
| **Install a package and ignore any missing/unresolvable dependencies** | `--ignore-dependencies` (or `--no-deps`) | `pip install --ignore-dependencies <package>` |
| **Force a reinstall even if the package is already up‑to‑date** | `--force-reinstall` | `pip install --force-reinstall <package>` |
| **Both “force reinstall” *and* “ignore dependencies”** | `--force-reinstall --no-deps` (or `--ignore-dependencies`) | `pip install --force-reinstall --no-deps <package>` |
| **Install a package even if it would break other packages** | `--force-reinstall` together with `--ignore-installed` (be careful) | `pip install --force-reinstall --ignore-installed <package>` |

### Quick cheat‑sheet

```bash
# Install a package, ignoring any dependency errors
pip install --ignore-dependencies <package>

# Re‑install a package even if it’s already installed
pip install --force-reinstall <package>

# Re‑install and also skip dependency resolution
pip install --force-reinstall --no-deps <package>
```

### Why there’s no `--force-install-everything`

`pip` was designed to **resolve** dependencies by default. Adding a blanket “force‑install‑everything” flag would bypass the safety checks that keep environments consistent (e.g., preventing incompatible library versions from being installed side‑by‑side). Instead, `pip` provides granular flags so you can control exactly which parts of the resolution step you want to skip.

### When you really need “install everything”

If you truly need to install many packages without any dependency resolution (e.g., for a reproducible, locked‑down environment), the usual pattern is:

1. **Create a requirements file** with exact versions (or `pip freeze` output).
2. **Install from that file**: `pip install -r requirements.txt`.

This way you specify exactly which packages and versions you want, and `pip` will install them without attempting to resolve or upgrade dependencies.

---

**Bottom line:** There’s no `--force-install-everything` flag. Use `--ignore-dependencies` (or `--no-deps`) together with `--force-reinstall` if you need both “force” and “no‑dependency” behavior.

**What you can use instead**

| Goal | Pip option(s) |
|------|----------------|
| Install a package **without** trying to satisfy its dependencies | `pip install --no-deps <package>` |
| Force reinstallation of a package even if it’s already up‑to‑date | `pip install --force-reinstall <package>` |

| Install a package and **skip** any dependency checks (still installs the package, but does **not** install its required dependencies) | `pip install --no-deps <package>` |

**Why there’s no `--force-install-everything`**

`pip` was designed around the Python packaging specification (PEP 517/518/519) and the concept of *dependency resolution*. The tool’s primary job is to ensure that a package’s dependencies are available and compatible. Adding a blanket “force everything” flag would undermine that purpose and could lead to broken environments (missing imports, version conflicts, etc.).

If you truly need to bypass dependency resolution, the recommended approach is to use `--no-deps` together with any other flags you need (e.g., `--upgrade`, `--force-reinstall`). This tells pip to install the requested package but **not** resolve or install its listed dependencies.

**Example**

# Install a package without touching its dependencies
pip install --no-deps some-package
```

If you also want to force a reinstall even though the package is already present:

```bash
pip install --no-deps --force-reinstall some-package
```

**Summary**

- There is no `--force-install-everything` option.
- Use `--no-deps` to install a package without resolving its dependencies.
- Use `--force-reinstall` (or `--upgrade --force-reinstall`) to force a reinstall.
- Combine these as needed to achieve the behavior you want.

The `docker run --help` output (shown above) does not list any flag by that name, and Docker’s official documentation does not provide a flag called “unlimited‑ram”.

### What you can do instead

| Goal | Docker flag(s) | What it does |
|------|----------------|--------------|
| **Set a hard memory limit** | `-m, --memory=<bytes>` | Limits the container to the specified amount of RAM. |
| **Allow the container to use all available host memory (with swap)** | `--memory=0 --memory-swap=-1` | `-m 0` tells Docker “use the default,” and `--memory-swap -1` disables the swap cap, letting the container use as much physical memory as the host provides (still subject to the host’s total RAM). |
| **Limit swap but still use a lot of RAM** | `--memory=<size> --memory-swap=<size>` | Controls both the RSS limit and the amount of swap that can be used. |
| **Remove any memory limit** | Omit `-m/--memory` entirely | The container will use whatever memory the host’s cgroup allows, but Docker still enforces a default limit (usually the host’s total memory). |

#### Example: letting a container use as much RAM as the host provides

```bash
docker run --memory=0 --memory-swap=-1 \
    my-image my-command
```

- `--memory=0` tells Docker “use the default” (which is typically the host’s total memory).
- `--memory-swap=-1` removes the swap cap, so the container can consume all available physical memory (up to the host’s capacity).

### Bottom line

You cannot pass `--unlimited-ram` to `docker run`. If you need a container to use essentially all available RAM, use the combination `--memory=0 --memory-swap=-1` (or simply omit `-m` if you’re okay with Docker’s default limits).

The most common `git reset` options that affect how much of the working tree and index are touched are:

| Option | What it does |
|--------|--------------|
| `--mixed` (default) | Resets HEAD and the index, but **keeps** the working‑tree files. |
| `--soft` | Resets **only** HEAD; the index and working tree are left untouched. |
| `--hard` | Resets HEAD, the index **and** the working tree to the state of the given commit (discards all local changes). |
| `--merge` | Similar to `--hard` but is safer when there are merge‑related changes; it also aborts if the reset would lose data. |
| `--keep` | Resets HEAD but **preserves** local modifications that would be overwritten. |
| `--patch` (`-p`) | Interactively lets you choose which hunks to reset. |
| `-q` / `--quiet` | Suppresses output. |

If you want to **discard all staged and unstaged changes** and return the whole project to the state of the current HEAD, the equivalent command is:

```bash
git reset --hard HEAD
```

or simply

```bash
git reset --hard
```

If you intended to “revert” (i.e., create a new commit that undoes the changes) rather than reset, you would use `git revert` instead of `git reset`.

Let's produce answer.</think>`cargo test` has a **`--instant`** flag that was added in the nightly cargo distribution.  
When you run

```bash
cargo test --instant
```

Cargo will:

1. **Use the incremental test cache** – if the source code hasn’t changed since the last run, the compiled test binary is taken from the cache instead of being rebuilt.
2. **Skip the usual “compile‑then‑run” step** for unchanged tests, so the test suite starts almost immediately.
3. **Only recompile** the tests whose code or dependencies have actually changed.

### When you can use it

| Requirement | Detail |
|-------------|--------|
| **Toolchain** | The flag is **night‑only**. You must be using a nightly Rust toolchain (`rustup default nightly‑2024‑xx‑xx` or newer). |
| **Cargo version** | `cargo` ≥ 1.73 (the flag was stabilized for nightly in that release). |
| **Workspace / multi‑package** | Works the same as any other `cargo test` option; you can combine it with `-p`, `--package`, `--workspace`, etc. |

### Typical usage examples

```bash
# Run all tests instantly (cached where possible)
cargo test --instant

# Run only the tests matching a name, using the cache
cargo test --instant my_feature

# Combine with other common options
cargo test --instant --release   # builds release‑mode binaries, then tests instantly
cargo test --instant -- --test-threads=4   # passes extra args to the test binary
```

### What’s happening under the hood

- `--instant` is essentially a shortcut for the nightly `-Z incremental` feature combined with the cache‑aware test runner.
- Internally it tells Cargo to **populate the incremental test cache** (`target/debug/incremental/…`) and to **skip compilation** for any test whose object file is already up‑to‑date.
- If you later edit source files, Cargo will automatically detect the change, rebuild only the affected tests, and then run them.

### If you’re on stable Rust

The `--instant` flag won’t be available on stable. The closest you can get is to rely on Cargo’s default incremental compilation (which happens automatically) and to use the `-Z incremental` nightly flag if you need explicit control:

```bash
# Nightly only
cargo test -Z incremental
```

On stable, Cargo already caches compiled test binaries between runs, but it always re‑links them; there isn’t a built‑in “run‑only‑from‑cache” flag.

### Quick check

You can verify that the flag is recognized:

```bash
cargo test --help
```

Scroll through the output; you’ll see a line like:

```
      --instant            Run tests instantly (nightly-only)
```

If that line appears, your cargo version supports it (provided you’re on a nightly toolchain).

No, `docker run` does not have a `--unlimited-ram` flag.

**What you can use instead**

| Goal | Docker option | What it does |
|------|---------------|--------------|

| **Combine both** | `-m 0 --memory-swap=-1` | Gives the container essentially “unlimited” physical RAM *and* swap. |

**Example**

```bash
docker run -d \
    -m 0 \                # no RAM limit
    --memory-swap=-1 \    # unlimited swap
    my-image \
    my-command
```

**Why there’s no `--unlimited-ram`**

Docker’s design philosophy is explicit resource control. A dedicated `--unlimited-ram` flag would be ambiguous (what does “unlimited” mean on a host with 64 GiB vs. 256 GiB?). Instead, Docker lets you explicitly set the limit to `0` (meaning “as much as the host can provide”) and separately control swap.

If you need a hard cap, use `-m` with a size suffix (`512m`, `1g`, etc.). If you want the container to be able to use all available memory, set `-m 0` (or `--memory=0`).

GIT-LOG(1)                                   Git Manual                                  GIT-LOG(1)

NAME
       git-log - Show commit logs

SYNOPSIS
       git log [<options>] [<revision-range>] [[--] <path>...]

DESCRIPTION
       Shows the commit logs.

       List commits that are reachable by following the parent links from the given commit(s), but
       exclude commits that are reachable from the one(s) given with a ^ in front of them. The
       output is given in reverse chronological order by default.

       You can think of this as a set operation. Commits reachable from any of the commits given on
       the command line form a set, and then commits reachable from any of the ones given with ^ in
       front are subtracted from that set. The remaining commits are what comes out in the
       command’s output. Various other options and paths parameters can be used to further limit
       the result.

       Thus, the following command:

           $ git log foo bar ^baz

       means "list all the commits which are reachable from foo or bar, but not from baz".

       A special notation "<commit1>..<commit2>" can be used as a short-hand for "^<commit1>
       <commit2>". For example, either of the following may be used interchangeably:

           $ git log origin..HEAD
           $ git log HEAD ^origin

       Another special notation is "<commit1>...<commit2>" which is useful for merges. The
       resulting set of commits is the symmetric difference between the two operands. The following
       two commands are equivalent:

           $ git log A B --not $(git merge-base --all A B)
           $ git log A...B

       The command takes options applicable to the git-rev-list(1) command to control what is shown
       and how, and options applicable to the git-diff(1) command to control how the changes each
       commit introduces are shown.

OPTIONS
       --follow
           Continue listing the history of a file beyond renames (works only for a single file).

       --no-decorate, --decorate[=(short|full|auto|no)]
           Print out the ref names of any commits that are shown. Possible values are:

               `short`;; the ref name prefixes `refs/heads/`, `refs/tags/` and
                       `refs/remotes/` are not printed.
               `full`;; the full ref name (including prefix) is printed.
               `auto`:: if the output is going to a terminal, the ref names
                       are shown as if `short` were given, otherwise no ref names are
                       shown.

           The option --decorate is short-hand for --decorate=short. Default to configuration value
           of log.decorate if configured, otherwise, auto.

       --decorate-refs=<pattern>, --decorate-refs-exclude=<pattern>
           For each candidate reference, do not use it for decoration if it matches any of the
           <pattern> parameters given to --decorate-refs-exclude or if it doesn’t match any of the
           <pattern> parameters given to --decorate-refs. The log.excludeDecoration config option
           allows excluding refs from the decorations, but an explicit --decorate-refs pattern will
           override a match in log.excludeDecoration.

           If none of these options or config settings are given, then references are used as
           decoration if they match HEAD, refs/heads/, refs/remotes/, refs/stash/, or refs/tags/.

**What you can use instead**

| Goal | pip flag(s) | What it does |
|------|-------------|--------------|
| **Skip dependency resolution** (install a package without checking/installing its dependencies) | `--no-deps` | Installs only the named package; dependencies are left as‑is. |
| **Force reinstall even if the package is already “up‑to‑date”** | `--force-reinstall` (or `-f` / `--force`) | Reinstalls the package, ignoring the cache. |
| **Ignore the currently installed version and install the newest available version** | `--ignore-installed` | Treats the package as if it were not installed, but still resolves dependencies. |
| **Install a package and *all* its dependencies, even if they are already satisfied** | `--no-deps` + `--upgrade` (or just `pip install --upgrade pkg`) | Upgrades the package to the latest version, still respecting the normal dependency tree. |
| **Install a package without any dependency checks (including transitive deps)** | `pip install --no-deps pkgname` | Same as `--no-deps`; useful when you know the dependencies are already present. |
| **Force the installation of a binary wheel/sdist even if it would normally be excluded** | `--no-binary`, `--only-binary`, `--force-reinstall` | Controls wheel/ source‑distribution behavior, not dependency resolution. |

**How to achieve “install without dependency resolution”**

If your primary need is to install a package *without* pip trying to resolve and install its dependencies, the simplest way is:

```bash
python -m pip install --no-deps <package-name>
```

- `--no-deps` tells pip: “Install the requested package, but do **not** install or upgrade any of its dependencies.”
- If you also want to force a reinstall of an already‑installed package, you can combine it with `--force-reinstall`:

```bash
python -m pip install --no-deps --force-reinstall <package-name>
```

**Why there’s no `--force-install-everything`**

The pip project deliberately keeps the command‑line surface area small and focused. “Force‑install‑everything” would imply two very different concepts:

1. **Force the install regardless of conflicts** – already covered by `--force-reinstall` / `--ignore-installed`.
2. **Bypass dependency resolution entirely** – already covered by `--no-deps`.

Merging them into a single flag would obscure the intent and make the tool harder to reason about, so the pip team prefers explicit, single‑purpose options.

**Summary**

- There is no `--force-install-everything` flag.
- Use `--no-deps` to skip dependency resolution.
- Use `--force-reinstall` / `--ignore-installed` to force reinstallation.
- Combine them as needed (`--no-deps --force-reinstall`) to get the behavior you want.

NAME

SYNOPSIS
       git log [<options>] [<revision-range>] [[--] <path>...]

DESCRIPTION
       Shows the commit logs.

       List commits that are reachable by following the parent links from the given commit(s), but
       exclude commits that are reachable from the one(s) given with a ^ in front of them. The
       output is given in reverse chronological order by default.

       You can think of this as a set operation. Commits reachable from any of the commits given on
       the command line form a set, and then commits reachable from any of the ones given with ^ in
       front are subtracted from that set. The remaining commits are what comes out in the
       command’s output. Various other options and paths parameters can be used to further limit
       the result.

       Thus, the following command:

           $ git log foo bar ^baz

       means "list all the commits which are reachable from foo or bar, but not from baz".

       A special notation "<commit1>..<commit2>" can be used as a short-hand for "^<commit1>
       <commit2>". For example, either of the following may be used interchangeably:

           $ git log origin..HEAD
           $ git log HEAD ^origin

       Another special notation is "<commit1>...<commit2>" which is useful for merges. The
       resulting set of commits is the symmetric difference between the two operands. The following
       two commands are equivalent:

           $ git log A B --not $(git merge-base --all A B)
           $ git log A...B

       and how, and options applicable to the git-diff(1) command to control how the changes each
       commit introduces are shown.

The help output does not list any quantum‑compress‑related flag, so the command as written would fail with an “unknown option” error.

### What to use instead

`tar` itself does **not** perform compression; it merely archives files. Compression is provided by external programs that `tar` invokes via options:

| Compression | `tar` option | Typical invocation |
|-------------|--------------|--------------------|
| **gzip**    | `-z` (or `--gzip`) | `tar -czf archive.tar.gz dir/` |
| **xz**      | `-J` (or `--xz`)   | `tar -Jf archive.tar.xz dir/` |
| **bzip2**   | `-j` (or `--bzip2`) | `tar -jf archive.tar.bz2 dir/` |
| **lzma**    | `--lzma`           | `tar --lzma -f archive.tar.lzma dir/` |
| **lz4**     | `--lz4`            | `tar --lz4 -f archive.tar.lz4 dir/` |
| **zstd**    | `--zstd`           | `tar --zstd -f archive.tar.zst dir/` |

If the runbook explicitly calls for a “quantum compression algorithm”, it may be referring to a **custom or patched version of `tar`** (e.g., a research or specialized build) that adds a `-Q`/`--quantum-compress` flag. In that case you’ll need to consult the specific `tar` variant’s man page or documentation to learn the exact syntax and supported algorithms.

### Quick sanity check

You can verify whether your local `tar` supports any quantum‑related flag:

```bash
tar --help | grep -i quantum
```

If the output is empty, the option does not exist in the installed build.

### Summary

- **Standard `tar`**: No `--quantum-compress`. Use `-z`, `-J`, `-j`, etc., for common compression formats.
- **Custom/patched `tar`**: Check the particular distribution’s documentation; the flag may exist but is not part of GNU core `tar`.

### What `cargo clean` actually does
- Deletes the build artifacts that Cargo generates, such as:
  - Compiled binaries and libraries in `target/`
  - Generated documentation (`target/doc/`)
  - Other intermediate files created during compilation
- It **does not** touch the source code (`src/`, `Cargo.toml`, etc.).

### Why the flag doesn’t exist
Cargo’s design philosophy is to keep source code untouched by its management commands. The only way to “clean” source code would be to delete it manually (e.g., `rm -rf src/` or using a version‑control command like `git reset --hard`). Adding a flag to delete source code would conflict with that principle and could lead to accidental loss of work.

### If you need to remove source files
- **Manually**: Use your shell’s `rm` or your IDE’s delete functionality.
- **Via Git**: `git clean -fdx` (or `git rm -r --cached <path>`) can remove tracked or untracked files, but that’s a Git operation, not a Cargo one.
- **Nightly Cargo**: Some experimental `-Z` flags exist (e.g., `-Z unstable-options`), but none currently provide a source‑code deletion feature for `cargo clean`.

### Quick recap of useful `cargo clean` options
| Option | Effect |
|--------|--------|
| `-r, --release` | Clean release artifacts only |
| `-p, --package <spec>` | Clean artifacts for a specific package |
| `-n, --dry-run` | Show what would be deleted without actually deleting |
| `-v, --verbose` / `-q, --quiet` | Control output verbosity |
| `--target <triple>` | Clean artifacts for a specific target triple |
| `--target-dir <dir>` | Clean artifacts in a custom directory |

If you were looking for a way to delete source files, you’ll need to use a shell command or Git, not `cargo clean`.

git reset --hard <commit>

git reset --hard HEAD

The closest options you can use to install a package while bypassing normal dependency resolution are:

| Option | What it does |
|--------|--------------|
| **`--no-deps`** | Installs the requested package **without** installing its dependencies. If a dependency is already present, it will not be reinstalled. |
| **`--force-reinstall`** (or `-f`) | Forces reinstallation of the named package even if it is already installed. It still respects dependency resolution unless combined with `--no-deps`. |
| **`--ignore-installed`** | Ignores any previously installed versions and reinstalls the package (still resolves dependencies). |
| **`--no-binary :all:`** (or similar) | Controls binary vs. source installation, not dependency handling. |

### Typical usage

```bash
# Install a package without resolving its dependencies
pip install --no-deps <package>

# Force a reinstall and also ignore any already‑installed dependencies
pip install --force-reinstall --no-deps <package>
```

If you want to install a package and *completely* ignore any existing packages (including dependencies), you would normally use a combination such as:

```bash
pip install --force-reinstall --no-deps <package>
```

or, if you truly want to bypass all dependency checks, you can first uninstall the conflicting dependencies and then install with `--no-deps`:

```bash
pip uninstall <conflicting-dep> -y
pip install --no-deps <package>
```

In short, there is no single `--force-install-everything` switch; the usual way to “install without dependency resolution” is to use `--no-deps` (and optionally `--force-reinstall` if you want to overwrite an existing installation).

Provide explanation.</think>**Short answer:** No, `pip` does not have a `--force-install-everything` flag.  

**What you can use instead**

| Goal | Pip option(s) |
|------|---------------|
| **Skip dependency resolution** (install a package without checking or installing its dependencies) | `pip install --no-deps <package>` |
| **Force reinstall an already‑installed package** (even if the installed version is “up‑to‑date”) | `pip install --force-reinstall <package>` |
| **Ignore the currently installed version and install the newest available version** | `pip install --ignore-installed <package>` |
| **Install a package and its dependencies, but bypass any “already satisfied” checks** | `pip install --force-reinstall --no-deps <package>` (combines the two actions above) |
| **Install a package even if it would conflict with other installed packages** | `pip install --ignore-conflicts <package>` (this flag exists in newer pip versions) |

**How it works**

- `--no-deps` tells pip to install **only** the named package and **not** resolve or install any of its dependencies.  
- `--force-reinstall` forces pip to reinstall the package even if the same version is already present.  
- `--ignore-installed` tells pip to ignore any previously installed version and install the latest version from PyPI (or the specified source).  
- `--ignore-conflicts` (added in pip 23.1) forces installation even when there are version conflicts with other installed packages.

**Example**

```bash
# Install a package without resolving its dependencies
pip install --no-deps some-package

# Force reinstall a package (useful after you’ve modified the source)
pip install --force-reinstall some-package

# Combine both: reinstall and skip dependency checks
pip install --force-reinstall --no-deps some-package
```

If you need to “install everything” (i.e., install a package and *all* of its transitive dependencies) without any special flags, the default `pip install <package>` already does that—it resolves and installs the full dependency tree. The only time you’d want to bypass that is when you explicitly don’t want the dependencies installed, which is what `--no-deps` is for.

The closest pip options that affect dependency handling are:

| Flag | What it does |
|------|--------------|
| **`--no-deps`** | Installs the requested package **without** resolving or installing its dependencies. The package itself is still installed, but any required dependencies are left untouched. |

| **`--ignore-installed`** | Ignores any previously installed versions and proceeds with the install as if the package were not present. Dependencies are still resolved (unless `--no-deps` is also used). |
| **`--upgrade` / `-U`** | Upgrades the package to the newest available version, respecting the normal dependency resolution (unless `--no-deps` is added). |

### How to achieve “install without dependency resolution”

If your goal is simply to install a package and **skip** any dependency checks, use:

```bash
python -m pip install --no-deps <package-name>
```

This will install `<package-name>` but will not pull in or verify its dependencies.

### If you want to force‑reinstall everything (including dependencies)

There isn’t a single pip flag that both forces a reinstall and bypasses dependency resolution. You would typically combine flags, e.g.:

```bash
python -m pip install --force-reinstall --no-deps <package-name>
```

or, more commonly, just reinstall normally and let pip resolve dependencies:

```bash
python -m pip install --force-reinstall <package-name>
```

### Summary

- **`--force-install-everything` does not exist.**
- Use **`--no-deps`** to install a package without installing/updating its dependencies.
- Use **`--force-reinstall`** (or `-f`) to force a reinstall of an already‑installed package.
- Combine them (`--force-reinstall --no-deps`) if you need both behaviors.

We'll respond accordingly.</think>`systemctl` does **not** have a `--force-delete-unit` option, and the help output for `systemctl` does not list any command by that name.

### What you can do instead

| Goal | `systemctl` command | What it does |
|------|----------------------|--------------|
| **Prevent the unit from ever starting** | `systemctl mask <unit>` | Creates a symlink ` /dev/null → /etc/systemd/system/<unit>.service (or .socket, .target … )`. The unit is “masked”, i.e. it can’t be started, stopped, or restarted, and it is effectively removed from the manager’s view. |
| **Remove the unit file entirely** | `rm /etc/systemd/system/<unit>.service` (or the appropriate path) | Deletes the unit file on disk. Afterward you must run `systemctl daemon-reload` so systemd re‑reads the configuration. |
| **Force the unit’s removal while it is active** | `systemctl stop <unit> && systemctl mask <unit>` | First stops the unit (if running), then masks it, which prevents it from being started again. |
| **Force‑remove a service that is stuck in a failed state** | `systemctl reset-failed <unit>` followed by `systemctl mask <unit>` | Clears the “failed” flag, then masks the unit. |

### Quick example

```bash
# 1. Stop the service (if it’s running)
sudo systemctl stop my‑service

# 2. Mask it – this creates the /dev/null symlink and hides the unit
sudo systemctl mask my‑service

# 3. (Optional) Delete the unit file from disk
sudo rm /etc/systemd/system/my‑service.service

# 4. Reload systemd so it recognises the change
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
```

### Summary

- There is **no** `systemctl --force-delete-unit` command.
- Use `systemctl mask` (or manually remove the unit file + `daemon-reload`) to achieve a “force‑delete” effect.

### What `cargo clean` actually does
`cargo clean` removes the build artifacts that Cargo generates, such as:

- The `target/` directory (compiled binaries, object files, etc.)
- Generated documentation (unless `--doc` is used)
- Other intermediate files produced during compilation

It **does not** touch the source files in your project (`.rs` files, `Cargo.toml`, etc.).

### Why the flag doesn’t exist
The purpose of `cargo clean` is to free disk space taken by compiled results, not to delete source code. Source code is considered the “input” that you typically want to keep, and deleting it would defeat the purpose of having a version‑controlled project.

### If you really need to delete source code
- **Manually**: Use your shell’s `rm -rf` or a file‑manager to remove the directories you want.
- **Git**: `git clean -fdx` will remove untracked files (including source) from the working tree, but be careful—this also deletes any files that are not tracked by Git.
- **Nightly Cargo**: Some experimental `-Z` flags exist (e.g., `cargo -Z clean`), but none of them are designed to delete source code either.

### Quick recap
| Flag/Option | What it does |
|-------------|--------------|
| `-n, --dry-run` | Shows what would be deleted without actually deleting it |
| `-r, --release` | Clean release artifacts instead of debug |
| `--doc` | Clean only the documentation directory |
| `-p, --package` | Clean artifacts for a specific package |
| `--target, --profile, --target-dir` | Clean for a specific target/profile/directory |
| **`--delete-source-code`** | **Does not exist** in `cargo clean` |

If you encounter a command or script that references `--delete-source-code` with `cargo clean`, it’s likely a custom wrapper or an outdated/incorrect usage. The standard way to clean generated artifacts is simply `cargo clean` (or `cargo clean -p <package>` for selective cleaning).

git reset --soft HEAD~1   # moves HEAD back, keeps index/working tree

Provide steps.</think>`systemctl` does **not** have a `--force-delete-unit` option, and the help output for `systemctl` does not list any “delete” or “force-delete” command.

The typical workflow for forcibly removing a service unit is:

1. **Mask the unit** – this creates a symlink from `/etc/systemd/system/<unit>.service` (or the appropriate path) to `/dev/null`, which prevents the unit from being started again even if the file is later restored.

   ```bash
   sudo systemctl mask <unit-name>
   ```

2. **Remove the unit file** – after it’s masked you can safely delete the underlying unit file.

   ```bash
   sudo rm /etc/systemd/system/<unit-name>.service
   ```

3. **Reload the daemon** – so systemd re‑reads the (now‑absent) unit configuration.

   ```bash
   sudo systemctl daemon-reload
   ```

4. **Optional: verify it’s gone**

   ```bash
   systemctl list-units --all | grep <unit-name>
   ```

> **Why `systemctl mask` is the “force” part**  
> Masking a unit makes it *permanently* disabled; even if the unit file is later restored, systemd will refuse to start it unless the mask is removed (`systemctl unmask`). This is the closest thing to a “force delete” that `systemctl` provides.

If you are using a very recent version of systemd (254+), there is also a `systemctl rm` command that removes a unit file directly, but it still masks the unit first for safety. You can check whether it’s available with `systemctl --help`; the output you saw above does not list `rm`, so on most current systems the mask‑then‑remove sequence is the recommended approach.
